description: Green Window is a team from Brazil working where agriculture meets Earth observation. Our name comes from the planting window: the months when a crop fits the local climate, shown in green in our tool. We turn NASA climate and terrain data into clear, explainable guidance that helps growers decide what to plant, when, and what should follow it, protecting their soil and adapting to a changing climate. We build tools that support the farmer's judgment with data they can trust.
summary: Field Shift is a browser tool that helps a grower decide what to plant, when, and what should follow it. The grower enters a location, what one bed or field receives over two years, and what matters most to them. The tool fetches ten years of NASA POWER climate data for that exact point, corrects temperature to the real altitude of the land using NASA SRTM terrain, and returns two things: a calendar showing in which months each crop fits the local climate, and three rotation strategies compared side by side, always including the current one. For every strategy it states why it is suggested, the evidence behind it, the benefits, and the risks that need local review. It matters because rotation advice is usually generic and climate data is too coarse for a mountain farm: at our test site in Andradas, Brazil, where coffee takes 63% of the harvested area, the altitude correction alone changes which crops fit. The tool supports the judgment of the grower and the agronomist. It does not replace it. Try it at https://lucasbnas435.github.io/nasa-space-apps-2026/
details:
What It Does

Field Shift answers one question for one piece of land: what can I grow here, when, and what should follow it?

The grower answers four questions on a single screen:

  1. What they grow: vegetables, annual crops (grains, potato), or perennial crops (coffee, banana).
  2. Where the land is: a coordinate copied from a map. Altitude is read automatically.
  3. What one bed or field receives today: up to six crops over two years.
  4. What matters most: growing each crop in the right climate, breaking pest and disease cycles, protecting the soil, irrigating less.

The tool returns:

  • The climate of the point: ten years of monthly rainfall, temperature and root-zone soil wetness, with the lowest rainfall of the ten years for each month, the months with frost on record, and the slope of the land.
  • A product-by-month calendar: for each crop, twelve squares colored green (inside its temperature range), yellow (at the edge, or heavy rain) or red (outside the range, or frost). Every square states its reason in plain words.
  • The municipal context: what is grown in the grower's municipality by harvested area, from the Brazilian statistics office, showing at a glance whether the region is a monoculture.
  • Three strategies compared on a 24-month timeline: the current rotation; the same crops with green manure in the idle windows; and a rotation that alternates plant families and fits crops to the climate. Each one shows why it is suggested, the evidence, the benefits over the current rotation, and the risks that need local review.
  • A closing box, "Limits of this tool", listing on screen what the tool does not model.

How It Works

Climate comes from NASA POWER as monthly values for the exact coordinate. The POWER grid cell is about 50 km wide and reports its own mean altitude, so the tool reads the real altitude of the point from NASA SRTM terrain and corrects temperature by the standard lapse rate of 0.65 °C per 100 m. At our test site the grid cell sits at 1,094 m and the field at about 1,330 m, a correction of -1.5 °C.

Two more NASA layers feed the strategies. Root-zone soil wetness from POWER (GWETROOT, from the MERRA-2 reanalysis) flags crop-months with dry soil. The slope, read from SRTM at the point and four neighbors about 330 m away, is combined with the rain that falls on bare soil into an erosion risk from low to very high, using the Embrapa relief classes. Erosion risk is shown on each strategy but does not change the score, so the ranking never depends on whether the elevation service answered.

Each crop has a plant family, a cycle length, a temperature range, and flags for frost sensitivity, sensitivity to heavy rain and protected cultivation. Each month a crop spends in the ground is classified as good, attention or risk. A rotation receives four scores from 0 to 1: climate fit, pest cycle break (the same plant family in sequence), soil protection (the share of rainfall that falls on an empty bed) and irrigation (a reference demand minus mean rainfall). The final score is weighted by the grower's four priorities, so two growers with the same land can get different recommendations.

The two alternatives are generated by transparent rules, not by a black box. One fills idle windows of two months or more with green manure. The other replaces a crop that repeats the previous plant family, or that falls outside its climate window, with the best-fitting crop of the same profile; when nothing fits, the bed rests under green manure.

Perennial crops do not rotate, so for coffee and banana the tool compares what happens between the rows: bare soil, green manure, or beans intercropped in the wettest window that fits the climate.

Benefits

  • Turns NASA global climate data into a decision a grower can act on, for their own point and altitude.
  • Shows the seasons of vulnerability before planting: at our test site, 10 of 24 vegetables fit all year, while frost on record from May to August closes the open-field window for peppers, squash, zucchini, cucumber and green beans.
  • Makes the cost of bare soil and of repeating the same plant family visible, in months and in millimeters of rain.
  • States its own limits, so it earns trust instead of overpromising.
  • Needs no login, no installation and no API key. English and Brazilian Portuguese.

What We Hope To Achieve

A tool a small or medium grower can open on a phone and use in five minutes, and that an agronomist can use as a starting point for a conversation. Next steps: review of the crop reference table by local agronomists against FAO ECOCROP and Embrapa planting calendars, finer soil moisture from SMAP and rainfall from GPM IMERG, field-scale slope from 30 m SRTM, an interactive map to pick the field, and planning many beds at once to keep supply steady through the year.

Limits

The crop reference table (temperature ranges and cycle lengths) holds general reference values and has not yet been reviewed by a local agronomist. Water demand uses a single reference of 4 mm per day. Soil wetness is a model estimate for the grid cell, not a field measurement. The slope from SRTM averages about 1 km and smooths out steep fields; the grower can type the real value. There is no soil analysis, pest history, price or market demand. For greenhouse crops the tool uses outside air temperature. For coffee and banana it looks only at the inter-row.

Tools

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework and no third-party code library. The model is a single JavaScript file of pure functions that runs in the browser and in Node.js, with a self-check that runs against live NASA POWER and IBGE data. The presentation was built with pptxgenjs, with screenshots taken with Puppeteer. Code is hosted on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license, and the tool is published with GitHub Pages.

Try it live (no login, works on a phone): https://lucasbnas435.github.io/nasa-space-apps-2026/
